kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-01.title: Work backwards
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-01.body:
At the end each boy has $30 \div 3 = 10$ balls. Anh received 4 and gave away 2, a net gain of 2, so he started with $10 - 2 = 8$.

**Answer: (A) 8**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-03.title: Check each ticket
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-03.body:
- 1022: only 4 digits ✗
- 22222: no digit above 2 ✓
- 102334: digits above 2 are 3, 3, 4 — three ✓
- 213343: 3, 3, 4, 3 — four ✗
- 3042531: 3, 4, 5, 3 — four ✗

Two winning tickets.

**Answer: (B) 2**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-04.title: Two halvings
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-04.body:
$F$ is the midpoint of $BC$, so $[ABF] = \frac12[ABC] = 48$. Triangles $AEF$ and $ABF$ have the same height from $F$, and $AE = \frac34 AB$ (since $AD = \frac12 AB$ and $DE = \frac14 AB$). So $[AEF] = \frac34\cdot 48 = 36$.

**Answer: (D) 36**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-05.title: Use thirds of a bag
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-05.body:
Each bag has 669 marbles; call one third of a bag a "part" (223 marbles). Bag A keeps 1 part; bag C has 3 parts plus 2 more parts = 5 parts. Ratio $1 : 5$.

**Answer: (D) 1:5**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-07.title: Where to put the straight move
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-07.body:
The grid has 4 columns and 5 rows, so the king must go 3 squares right and 4 squares down. Every move goes at most one row down, so at least 4 moves are needed, and 4 moves suffice: each move goes down one row, and exactly 3 of them also go one column right (diagonal moves) while one goes straight down.

A shortest route is determined by which of the 4 moves is the straight one: 4 routes.

**Answer: (B) 4**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-08.title: Maximise the sum
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-08.body:
We want $KAN + GA + ROO$ as large as possible:
$$KAN + GA + ROO = 100(K + R) + 11A + 11O + 10G + N.$$
Give the largest digits to the largest coefficients: $K, R = 9, 8$ (200-coefficient total), then $A, O = 7, 6$, then $G = 5$, then $N = 4$:
$$1700 + 11\cdot 13 + 50 + 4 = 1897.$$
E.g. $974 + 57 + 866 = 1897$. The least value is $2007 - 1897 = 110$.

**Answer: (B) 110**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-09.title: Strips cut by strips
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-09.body:
The four lines from $A$ divide the triangle into 5 "fans" from $A$. Each line from $B$ crosses every fan, cutting it into one more piece: the 4 lines from $B$ cut each fan into 5 pieces. Total $5\cdot 5 = 25$ (with 2 lines each: $3\cdot 3 = 9$ ✓).

**Answer: (B) 25**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-09.title: Count by adding lines
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-09.body:
Start with the 5 pieces from $A$'s lines. Each line from $B$ crosses the 4 lines from $A$, so it is cut into 5 segments, each splitting a region in two: $+5$ regions per line. $5 + 4\cdot 5 = 25$.

**Answer: (B) 25**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-10.title: Only one group can be right
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-10.body:
The three statements contradict each other, so at most one group tells the truth, and since there are nobles, exactly one group does — all others are liars.
- If the 2 people were right, there would be 10 liars, not 2. ✗
- If the 4 people were right, there would be 8 liars, not 4. ✗
- If the 6 people were right, there are 6 liars ✓.

So there are 6 liars.

**Answer: (C) 6**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-11.title: Watch the floor and the ceiling
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-11.body:
The floor and the ceiling slope down towards the right; the door sections have vertical sides and sloping top and bottom edges. A section turns about a vertical hinge, so every point of it keeps its height while it moves closer to the hinge side (seen across the hallway).

- **Lower section:** its bottom edge lies on the floor. If the hinge is on the left, the points of the bottom edge move to the left, where the floor is higher — the door scrapes the floor. With the hinge on the right they move right, where the floor is lower: it opens freely.
- **Upper section:** its top edge is at the ceiling. With the hinge on the right its points move right, where the ceiling is lower — it jams. With the hinge on the left they move to where the ceiling is higher: fine.

So: hinges above on the left, below on the right.

**Answer: (C) above left, below right**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-12.title: Three arcs
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-12.body:
Outside the house the dog can sweep $\frac34$ of a circle of radius 10 around the corner: length $\frac34\cdot 2\pi\cdot 10 = 15\pi$.

Going around the 6 m wall leaves $4$ m of rope: a quarter circle of radius 4, length $2\pi$. Going around the 4 m wall leaves 6 m: a quarter circle of radius 6, length $3\pi$. These two quarter circles meet exactly at the far corner of the house ($4 + 6 = 10$).

The outer boundary of the region has length $15\pi + 2\pi + 3\pi = 20\pi$ m.

**Answer: (A) $20\pi$**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-13.title: Name the sides
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-13.body:
Let the triangle have side $a$ and the removed equilateral corner side $b$. The trapezoid has sides $a$ (long base), $b$ (short base) and two legs $a - b$.

Placing two copies side by side (one turned upside down, joined along a leg) gives a parallelogram with sides $a + b$ and $a - b$. Its perimeter is $2(a + b) + 2(a - b) = 4a$.

$4a - 3a = a = 10$ cm, so the triangle's perimeter is $30$ cm (whatever $b$ is).

**Answer: (B) 30 cm**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-14.title: Powers of 2 survive
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-14.body:
After the first erasing only positions divisible by 2 remain, after the second only positions divisible by 4, and so on. The last letter left is at the position that is the largest power of 2 not exceeding $20\cdot 8 = 160$, namely $128$.

$128 = 16\cdot 8$ is the 8th letter of the 16th KANGAROO: **O**.

**Answer: (E) O**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-17.title: Count routes to every crossing
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-17.body:
Write at each crossing the number of ways to reach it: it is the sum of the numbers at the crossing above it, to its left, and diagonally up-left (where such streets exist). Row by row from the top (the triangle has legs of 4 blocks):
$$\begin{array}{ccccc}1\\1&2\\1&4&6\\1&6&16&22\\1&8&30&68&90\end{array}$$
For example $16 = 4 + 6 + 6$ and $68 = 16 + 22 + 30$. The rightmost corner gets $\mathbf{90}$.

**Answer: (D) 90**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-19.title: Straight parts and arcs
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-19.body:
The centre stays at distance $r$ (the coin's radius) from the hexagon. Along each side it moves parallel to the side: $6\cdot 1 = 6$ cm. At each corner it turns around the vertex on an arc of radius $r$; the six turning angles add up to $360^\circ$, so the arcs together form one full circle of radius $r$, length $2\pi r$.

With diameter 1 cm, $r = \frac12$ cm, and the path has length $6 + 2\pi\cdot\frac12 = 6 + \pi$ cm.

**Answer: (B) $6+\pi$**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-20.title: Exponents of 2, 3 and 5
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-20.body:
Only the primes 2, 3, 5 are needed: $A = 2^a3^b5^c$.
- $10A = 2^{a+1}3^b5^{c+1}$ is a square: $a+1$, $b$, $c+1$ even.
- $6A = 2^{a+1}3^{b+1}5^c$ is a cube: $a+1$, $b+1$, $c$ divisible by 3.

Smallest choices: $a + 1 = 6 \Rightarrow a = 5$; $b$ even with $b + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod 3$: $b = 2$; $c$ odd and divisible by 3: $c = 3$.

$A = 2^5\cdot3^2\cdot5^3$ has $(5+1)(2+1)(3+1) = 72$ divisors.

**Answer: (D) 72**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-21.title: Count by cycle structure
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-21.body:
Think of "who gives to whom" as arrows; everyone has one arrow out and one in, and nobody points to themselves. The arrows form cycles of length at least 2:
- one 5-cycle: $4! = 24$ ways;
- a 3-cycle and a 2-cycle: choose the pair, $\binom52 = 10$, and the 3-cycle can go 2 ways: $20$.

Total $24 + 20 = 44$.

**Answer: (C) 44**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-21.title: Derangement recursion
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-21.body:
The number $D_n$ of such arrangements satisfies $D_n = (n-1)(D_{n-1} + D_{n-2})$ with $D_1 = 0$, $D_2 = 1$: $D_3 = 2$, $D_4 = 9$, $D_5 = 4(9 + 2) = 44$.

**Answer: (C) 44**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-22.title: Everything in terms of the radius
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-22.body:
Let the circle have radius $r$.
- The big triangle has inradius $r$, so its side is $2\sqrt3\,r$ and $S_1 = 3\sqrt3\,r^2$.
- The small triangle has circumradius $r$, so its side is $\sqrt3\,r$ and $S_2 = \frac{3\sqrt3}{4}r^2$.
- The hexagon consists of 6 equilateral triangles of side $r$: $S_3 = \frac{3\sqrt3}{2}r^2$.

Then $S_1 S_2 = \frac{27}{4}r^4 = S_3^2$, so $S_3 = \sqrt{S_1 S_2}$. (B gives $\frac{15\sqrt3}{8}r^2$, C gives $\frac{9\sqrt3}{4}r^2$, E gives $\frac{15\sqrt3}{4}r^2$ — all wrong.)

**Answer: (A) $S_3 = \sqrt{S_1\times S_2}$**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-22.title: Ratios
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-22.body:
The small triangle has circumradius $r$, hence inradius $\frac r2$; the big one has inradius $r$. So the big triangle is the small one enlarged by factor 2: $S_1 = 4S_2$. The hexagon is the small triangle plus three caps, and each cap (a triangle with two hexagon sides) has the same area as one of the three triangles into which the centre cuts the small triangle; so $S_3 = 2S_2$. Hence $S_3^2 = 4S_2^2 = S_1S_2$.

**Answer: (A) $S_3 = \sqrt{S_1\times S_2}$**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-23.title: Fuel limits the speed
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-23.body:
Fuel per km is $kv$. The tank holds $80\cdot k\cdot 100 = 8000k$. Driving 100 km at constant speed $v$ uses $100kv$, so we need $100kv \le 8000k$, i.e. $v \le 80$ km/h.

(Varying the speed does not help: faster stretches cost more fuel per km than slower stretches save, so for a fixed amount of fuel the fastest way is a constant speed.) At 80 km/h the 100 km take $1.25$ h $= 1$ h 15 min: arrival at **22:15**.

**Answer: (B) 22:15**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-24.title: Count the favourable triples
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-24.body:
There are $\binom{12}{3} = 220$ equally likely triples.
- A, same colour: 4 colours, 1 triple each: $4$.
- B, numbers 1, 2, 3: choose the colour of each number: $4^3 = 64$.
- C, three different colours: choose 3 colours ($4$ ways) and one of 3 cards in each: $4\cdot 27 = 108$.
- D, same number: 3 numbers, $\binom43 = 4$ ways each: $12$.

C is the most probable.

**Answer: (C) The three cards are of three different colours.**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-b1.title: Triangle inequality twice
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-b1.body:
The string of length $x$ next to the centre of the web is a side of two small triangles:
- one with the other sides 9 and 5: $x < 9 + 5 = 14$;
- one with the other sides 5 and 17: $x > 17 - 5 = 12$.

So $12 < x < 14$ and the integer $x$ is $13$.

**Answer: (B) 13**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-b2.title: Only one factorisation
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-b2.body:
If there are $N$ diamonds in $k \ge 2$ necklaces of $m \ge 2$ diamonds, then $N = km$. Knowing $N$ fixes $k$ only if $N$ has exactly one factorisation into two factors $\ge 2$ (as an ordered pair!). If $N = km$ with $k \ne m$ we could swap them; so the only factorisation must be $k = m = p$ with $p$ prime, i.e. $N = p^2$ (for $N = p^3$ we would also have $p\cdot p^2$).

The only square of a prime between 200 and 300 is $289 = 17^2$, so there are 17 necklaces.

**Answer: (B) 17**

kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-b3.title: Measure along the diagonal
kangaroo-ca-2007-g0910-b3.body:
Let the radii be $r$ and $R$. The small circle touches the two sides at one corner, so its centre is $(r, r)$ — at distance $r\sqrt2$ from that corner along the diagonal. Likewise the other centre is $R\sqrt2$ from the opposite corner. The centres are $r + R$ apart (the circles touch). Along the diagonal of length $\sqrt2$:
$$r\sqrt2 + (r + R) + R\sqrt2 = \sqrt2 \;\Rightarrow\; (r+R)(1+\sqrt2) = \sqrt2,$$
$$r + R = \frac{\sqrt2}{1+\sqrt2} = \sqrt2(\sqrt2 - 1) = 2 - \sqrt2.$$
It does not depend on the ratio of the radii.

**Answer: (D) $2-\sqrt2$**
